title: Nvidia's Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC outscores the top human at IOI 2026 under match constraints
subtitle: The 550B-parameter model scored 535.4 out of 600 on the International Olympiad in Informatics problem set — ahead of the top official contestant's 498.27 and well above the gold threshold.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Nvidia researchers on September 3 published results showing Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC scoring 535.4 out of 600 on the IOI 2026 problem set — above the gold threshold of 361.12 and ahead of the top official human contestant's 498.27. The evaluation was run under matched competition constraints: same time budget, same internet-access rules, same submission limits. The system was not an official IOI contestant, so the score is not on the official leaderboard, but it is the first time an AI has cleared the top human's mark on a full IOI paper.

The recipe is worth reading closely. Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC is a 550B-parameter model with 55B active parameters, produced by supervised fine-tuning — no code-specific reinforcement learning — on top of the base Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B. Training data came from 22,000 curated problems and 1.2 million reasoning traces generated by DeepSeek-V4-Flash. At inference, the system uses GenCorrect, an iterative strategy that samples diverse solutions and refines them against feedback from prior submissions — the same submission-and-revise loop the human contestants get.

The larger context is that IOI is the last competitive-programming benchmark where humans still held. Codeforces, LiveCodeBench, HumanEval, MATH, GPQA — those fell across 2025 and early 2026. IOI held because the problems are novel, algorithmically dense and time-boxed against subtask scoring. Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC did not beat the field marginally; it beat the top scorer by 37 points in a system with a 600-point ceiling. Two years after the first AI hit a Codeforces expert rating, the frontier for "can a model out-code a top human" is essentially closed for structured contest formats.

For learners, the honest takeaway is not "stop learning to code." It is "the useful contest is shifting." A gold-medal human at IOI is not just fast — they carry a compressed catalog of algorithms and can pattern-match a novel problem to a known technique. That skill is still exactly the one that lets you tell whether a model's answer is right when the stakes matter. The economically valuable version of contest programming is now judgment under time pressure, not raw solve rate; the model can do the second.
